title: A Dark Matter Detector Catches the Sun's Faintest Neutrinos
hook: XENONnT was built to find dark matter. Instead it made the first keV-scale measurement of solar neutrinos scattering off electrons — the lowest-energy neutrino detection to date.
key_points: XENONnT reports the first solar neutrino measurement via elastic neutrino-electron scattering in a dark matter experiment.
It covers electron recoils from 1 to 140 keV, reaching neutrinos with energies down to 17 keV.
That is the lowest energy threshold achieved for any neutrino detection so far.
Exposure was 2.46 tonne-years across the first two science runs; the background-only hypothesis is rejected at 5.0 sigma.
The measured pp neutrino flux is (10.2 +/- 2.0) x 10^10 per cm^2 per second.
That is higher than but statistically consistent with Borexino's earlier value, differing by 1.9 sigma.
content_html: XENONnT is a three-tonne tank of liquid xenon buried under a mountain, designed to catch a dark matter particle nudging a xenon nucleus. Its exquisite sensitivity to tiny, rare energy deposits turns out to be useful for something else entirely: watching neutrinos from the Sun bounce off electrons.
extra_html: The collaboration reports the first measurement of low-energy solar neutrinos through elastic neutrino-electron scattering in a dark matter experiment, using 2.46 tonne-years of exposure from its first two science runs. Looking at electron recoils between 1 and 140 keV, the detector is sensitive to neutrinos with energies down to 17 keV — the lowest energy threshold reached for any neutrino detection to date. The background-only hypothesis is rejected at 5.0 sigma, and the inferred flux of pp neutrinos, produced in the very first step of the Sun's fusion chain, is (10.2 +/- 2.0) x 10^10 per square centimetre per second: higher than Borexino's earlier figure but consistent with it at 1.9 sigma. Together with recent detections of coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering from solar boron-8 neutrinos, the authors argue liquid xenon is becoming a serious neutrino technology, not just a dark matter one.

related.title: Catching the Ghost Particle
related.hook: Trillions of neutrinos stream through your body every second, yet they almost never touch anything. To catch even a few, physicists build some of the most audacious detectors ever conceived.

related.title: JUNO's First Look at Shape-Shifting Neutrinos
related.hook: A giant detector buried under China caught neutrinos changing identity mid-flight — and in just 59 days made one of the sharpest measurements yet of the ghost particle's habits.

related.title: What Powers the Sun
related.hook: The Sun isn't burning like a fire — it's fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, and a sliver of mass turning into pure energy is what lights up our sky.

related.title: A Dark Matter Detector That Asks Which Way the Hit Came From
related.hook: Neutrons and dark matter can leave identical-looking recoils. MIMAC's answer: reconstruct the direction of each recoil and check whether it points where dark matter should come from.

flashcards.prompt: What are pp neutrinos, and why are they hard to detect?
flashcards.back_html: They come from the first step of the Sun's proton-proton fusion chain. They carry very low energies, so the recoils they produce sit near or below most detectors' thresholds.

flashcards.prompt: Why is it notable that a dark matter detector made this measurement?

choices.text: The same liquid-xenon technology built for rare dark matter recoils turns out to work as a low-threshold neutrino observatory
It proves dark matter is made of neutrinos
It shows the Sun emits far more neutrinos than models predict

flashcards.explanation_html: The collaboration frames the result as a milestone toward a next-generation multipurpose liquid-xenon observatory serving both dark matter and neutrino physics.

flashcards.prompt: How does XENONnT's pp flux compare with Borexino's earlier measurement?
flashcards.back_html: Larger, but statistically consistent — the two differ by 1.9 sigma.
